traditions.name: Non-denominational Evangelical Churches
traditions.summary: Independent congregations that carry no denominational label, typically evangelical in belief and often contemporary or charismatic in worship. Independent 'Bible churches' existed long before, but the category grew sharply from the 1970s with the Jesus Movement, the church-growth and 'seeker-sensitive' models and the megachurch, until in the United States it became one of the largest Protestant groupings. Similar independent churches are now common across Africa, Latin America and Asia.
distinctives: No denominational affiliation; each congregation is self-governing, sometimes linked loosely through networks or associations
Short evangelical statements of faith rather than historic confessions
Contemporary worship with bands and projected songs
Many of the largest US megachurches, such as Lakewood Church (Houston) and North Point Community Church (Atlanta), belong to this category
Multi-site campuses and online services led by a founding or senior pastor

profile.authority: The Bible as the inspired and authoritative Word of God, usually set out in a brief local statement of faith; historic creeds are respected but seldom formally adopted.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through personal faith in Jesus Christ, with emphasis on a conscious decision to follow him ('being born again').
profile.sacraments: Usually called ordinances: believer's baptism (generally by immersion) and the Lord's Supper as a memorial, often held monthly or less often.
profile.eschatology: Christ's personal return; many congregations hold a premillennial and pre-tribulation view, though positions vary.
profile.governance: Congregational independence, in practice often led by a senior pastor with a board of elders or trustees.
profile.worship: Informal services centred on contemporary music and a practical sermon; many are openly charismatic, others are not.

traditions.status: Active and growing; in US religious surveys non-denominational Protestants are now among the largest Protestant groups.

traditions.name: Reformed Baptists (1689 Confessional)
traditions.summary: A movement of Calvinistic Baptist churches that hold to the Second London Baptist Confession of Faith (1677, adopted by an assembly in 1689). It continues the seventeenth-century Particular Baptist tradition, but as a distinct movement it grew from the Reformed revival of the 1950s and 1960s, helped by the Banner of Truth Trust and by Spurgeon's legacy, in Britain, the United States, South Africa and elsewhere.
distinctives: Subscription to the Second London Baptist Confession of 1689
A Baptist covenant theology ('1689 federalism') distinct from Presbyterian covenant theology
The regulative principle of worship
Plural eldership with male elders and deacons
Observance of the Lord's Day as the Christian Sabbath
Associations such as ARBCA (1997) in North America

profile.authority: Scripture alone as the sufficient and infallible rule, summarised in the 1689 Confession, which opens with its chapter on Scripture.
profile.salvation: The doctrines of grace: unconditional election, particular redemption, effectual calling and perseverance, with justification by faith alone.
profile.sacraments: Two ordinances: baptism of professing believers by immersion and the Lord's Supper, in which believers receive Christ spiritually by faith.
profile.eschatology: Mostly amillennial or postmillennial, with Christ's return, resurrection and final judgement.
profile.governance: Self-governing congregations led by elders and deacons, cooperating in associations.
profile.worship: Simple services of Scripture reading, prayer, psalms and hymns, and expository preaching.
profile.canon: The 66-book Protestant canon; the Apocrypha is excluded as not inspired.

traditions.status: Active; a small but internationally connected movement of confessional churches.

traditions.name: Primitive Baptists
traditions.summary: American 'Old School' Baptists who separated from the missionary Baptists in the 1820s and 1830s. The Kehukee Association in North Carolina condemned missionary societies in 1827, and the Black Rock Address (Maryland, 1832) rejected mission boards, Sunday schools, theological seminaries and other 'modern' institutions as having no warrant in Scripture. They hold a strong doctrine of predestination and keep simple, older forms of worship.
distinctives: Rejection of missionary societies, Sunday schools and seminaries as unscriptural
Strong predestinarian Calvinism
A cappella singing, in some areas from shape-note books
Foot washing with the Lord's Supper
Elders who are often unsalaried and self-supporting
Independent churches linked by associations and correspondence

profile.authority: Scripture alone; many associations adhere to the London Baptist Confession or their own articles of faith.
profile.salvation: God's elect are saved by his sovereign grace; outward means such as missions do not cause regeneration, which is God's direct work.
profile.sacraments: Ordinances of believer's baptism by immersion, the Lord's Supper with unleavened bread and wine, and foot washing.
profile.eschatology: Generally amillennial, with the resurrection and final judgement at Christ's return.
profile.governance: Independent congregations led by elders, gathered in local associations.
profile.worship: Plain, unaccompanied singing, extempore preaching and monthly meetings in many rural churches.
profile.canon: The 66-book Protestant canon, traditionally the King James Version.

traditions.status: Active but small and largely rural, mainly in the American South and Appalachia; several sub-groups exist.

traditions.name: Old Order Mennonites
traditions.summary: Conservative Mennonites who resisted innovations such as Sunday schools, English-language preaching, revival meetings and new technology. The movement began with Jacob Wisler in Indiana and Ohio (1872), followed by Abraham Martin in Ontario (1889) and Jonas Martin in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania (1893). Most groups still drive horse and buggy, though some (such as the Weaverland Conference) allow plain black cars.
distinctives: Separation from the world in dress, technology and language
Services in Pennsylvania German
Horse-and-buggy transport in most groups
Ministers chosen by lot
Meetinghouses without Sunday schools or musical instruments
Close-knit farming communities

profile.authority: Scripture, read through the Dordrecht Confession (1632) and the community's Ordnung (rules of practice).
profile.salvation: Salvation by God's grace, received by faith and shown in obedience, humility and separation from the world.
profile.sacraments: Ordinances: adult baptism by pouring, the Lord's Supper twice a year, foot washing and the holy kiss.
profile.eschatology: Christ's return, resurrection and judgement, without detailed millennial schemes.
profile.governance: Bishops, ministers and deacons chosen by lot from among the men of the congregation; conferences keep a common Ordnung.
profile.worship: Slow unaccompanied hymn singing, long sermons and silent prayer in plain meetinghouses.
profile.canon: The 66-book Protestant canon, usually the Luther Bible or King James Version.

traditions.status: Active and growing through large families, chiefly in Pennsylvania, Ontario, Ohio and Indiana.

traditions.name: Mennonite Brethren
traditions.summary: A Mennonite renewal church founded on 6 January 1860 in the Molotschna colony in the Russian Empire (now Ukraine), when eighteen men signed a document of secession calling for a converted membership. Influenced by German Pietism through the preacher Eduard Wüst, and by Baptists, they adopted baptism by immersion. Emigrants took the church to North America from the 1870s, and missions spread it to India, the Congo and beyond.
distinctives: Personal conversion as the condition of membership
Baptism by immersion
Evangelical and Pietist warmth within Anabaptist teaching
Strong missionary work since the late nineteenth century
Global fellowship through ICOMB (International Community of Mennonite Brethren)

profile.authority: Scripture as the final authority, expressed in the Mennonite Brethren Confession of Faith.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through faith in Christ, shown in a converted life and discipleship.
profile.sacraments: Ordinances of believer's baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper as a memorial; foot washing in some places.
profile.eschatology: Christ's return, resurrection and judgement; views on the millennium vary.
profile.governance: Congregational, with national and provincial conferences.
profile.worship: Evangelical services with singing, preaching and testimony; strong choral tradition among Russian Mennonite descendants.

traditions.status: Active worldwide, with large conferences in India, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, North America and Latin America.

traditions.name: Wisconsin Evangelical Lutheran Synod (WELS)
traditions.summary: A confessional Lutheran church founded in Milwaukee in 1850 by German immigrant pastors led by John Muehlhaeuser. Initially moderate, it became strictly confessional under Adolf Hoenecke and joined the Synodical Conference with the Missouri Synod in 1872. It broke fellowship with Missouri in 1961 over doctrinal differences, especially on church fellowship, and leads the Confessional Evangelical Lutheran Conference founded in 1993.
distinctives: Strict doctrine of fellowship: no shared worship or prayer without full doctrinal agreement
Close communion
Full subscription to the Book of Concord
Inerrancy of Scripture
Men only in the pastoral office and in roles of authority over men
Large system of Lutheran schools

profile.authority: Scripture as the inerrant Word of God, with unconditional subscription to the Lutheran Confessions in the Book of Concord (1580).
profile.salvation: Justification by grace alone through faith alone in Christ, proclaimed through Law and Gospel.
profile.sacraments: Baptism, including infants, and the Lord's Supper with the true body and blood of Christ really present, as means of grace.
profile.eschatology: Amillennial; Christ's visible return, resurrection and final judgement.
profile.governance: Synodical structure with a president, districts and a biennial convention; congregations call their pastors.
profile.worship: Lutheran liturgy and hymnody from Christian Worship (2021).

traditions.status: Active; one of the larger conservative Lutheran churches in the United States, with partner churches abroad.

traditions.name: Orthodox Presbyterian Church
traditions.summary: A small conservative Presbyterian church founded on 11 June 1936 in Philadelphia by J. Gresham Machen and others who had been removed from the northern Presbyterian Church for opposing theological liberalism. It is closely linked with Westminster Theological Seminary (1929), where Cornelius Van Til and John Murray taught, and is known for strict adherence to the Westminster Standards.
distinctives: Founded in the Fundamentalist–Modernist controversy
Strict subscription to the Westminster Confession and Catechisms
Presuppositional apologetics (Cornelius Van Til)
Male-only ministers and elders
Strong emphasis on foreign missions, e.g. in Eritrea, Uganda and Japan
Member of NAPARC

profile.authority: Scripture as the inerrant Word of God, with the Westminster Confession and Larger and Shorter Catechisms as subordinate standards.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace alone through faith alone, within Reformed covenant theology and predestination.
profile.sacraments: Baptism of believers and their children, and the Lord's Supper in which Christ is spiritually present to faith.
profile.eschatology: Mostly amillennial; Christ's return, resurrection and last judgement.
profile.governance: Presbyterian: sessions, presbyteries and a general assembly.
profile.worship: Reformed worship following the regulative principle, with psalms and hymns and expository preaching.
profile.canon: The 66-book Protestant canon; the Apocrypha is excluded.

traditions.status: Active; a small church of a few hundred congregations, mainly in the United States.

traditions.name: Free Church of Scotland
traditions.summary: Formed at the Disruption of 18 May 1843, when about a third of the ministers of the Church of Scotland, led by Thomas Chalmers, left over the state's interference in calling ministers (patronage). Most of the Free Church joined the United Presbyterians in 1900, but a minority, strongest in the Highlands and Islands, continued as the Free Church of Scotland. A further split in 2000 created the Free Church of Scotland (Continuing).
distinctives: Spiritual independence of the church from the state
Westminster Confession as the subordinate standard
Exclusive psalmody until 2010, when hymns and instruments were permitted
Strong Highland and Gaelic heritage
Observance of the Lord's Day

profile.authority: Scripture as the supreme rule, with the Westminster Confession of Faith as the subordinate standard.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace alone through faith in Christ, in Reformed covenant theology.
profile.sacraments: Baptism, including infants of believers, and the Lord's Supper with Christ spiritually present, traditionally after preparatory services.
profile.eschatology: Christ's return, resurrection and final judgement; amillennial and postmillennial views both held.
profile.governance: Presbyterian: kirk sessions, presbyteries and a General Assembly.
profile.worship: Reformed worship centred on preaching; psalms (often unaccompanied) and, since 2010, hymns at congregational discretion.

traditions.status: Active; around a hundred congregations, mostly in Scotland, with church planting in cities.

traditions.name: Reformed Presbyterian Churches (Covenanters)
traditions.summary: Heirs of the Scottish Covenanters who refused the Revolution Settlement of 1690 because it did not uphold the National Covenant (1638) and the Solemn League and Covenant (1643). Followers of the martyrs Richard Cameron (killed 1680) and James Renwick (executed 1688) met in 'societies' until John McMillan and Thomas Nairn formed the Reformed Presbytery in 1743. Reformed Presbyterian churches now exist in Scotland, Ireland, North America and Australia.
distinctives: Covenanting: public covenants binding church and nation to Christ
Christ's mediatorial kingship over the nations as well as the church
Exclusive singing of psalms without instruments
Historic political dissent from constitutions that do not acknowledge Christ
Close communion

profile.authority: Scripture, with the Westminster Confession and Catechisms and each church's own Testimony as subordinate standards.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace alone through faith, in Reformed covenant theology.
profile.sacraments: Baptism of believers and their children, and the Lord's Supper with Christ spiritually present.
profile.eschatology: Christ's return and judgement; postmillennial hope for the nations has been prominent.
profile.worship: Unaccompanied singing of the psalms only, Scripture reading, prayer and preaching.

traditions.status: Active but small; the largest body is the Reformed Presbyterian Church of North America (RPCNA).

traditions.name: International Churches of Christ
traditions.summary: A movement that grew from the 'discipling' method of Chuck Lucas's Crossroads Church of Christ in Gainesville, Florida, and was launched by Kip McKean at the Lexington (later Boston) Church of Christ in 1979. It spread fast through planted churches in world cities and became separate from the mainline Churches of Christ. After McKean's departure (2001–2002) and an open letter by Henry Kriete (2003) criticising authoritarian practices, it was reorganised in 2006 as a cooperation of autonomous churches.
distinctives: One-to-one discipling relationships
Baptism by immersion for forgiveness of sins after a commitment to be a disciple
Rapid planting of churches in major cities
Large campus ministries
HOPE worldwide, a charity founded in 1991
Reorganised in 2006 after criticism of its earlier hierarchy

profile.authority: The Bible alone as the guide, in the Restorationist tradition.
profile.salvation: Faith, repentance, confession and baptism by immersion for the forgiveness of sins, followed by a life of discipleship.
profile.sacraments: Baptism of disciples by immersion and the weekly Lord's Supper as a memorial.
profile.eschatology: Christ's return, resurrection and judgement; little speculation on the millennium.
profile.governance: Autonomous congregations led by evangelists and elders, cooperating regionally and globally.
profile.worship: Sunday services with singing, communion and preaching, plus midweek groups.

traditions.status: Active in many countries; Kip McKean's separate International Christian Church formed in 2006.

traditions.name: Congregação Cristã no Brasil
traditions.summary: Brazil's oldest Pentecostal church, founded in 1910 by Louis (Luigi) Francescon, an Italian immigrant from Chicago who had been part of William Durham's Pentecostal mission. Beginning among Italian immigrants in São Paulo and Paraná, it grew into one of Brazil's largest Protestant churches while keeping a strikingly austere style: no paid clergy, no broadcasting and no organised evangelistic campaigns.
distinctives: Unpaid ministry of elders (anciãos) and deacons
No radio, television or public evangelistic campaigns
No tithing; voluntary anonymous offerings
Men and women sit apart and women wear veils
Large church orchestras and the hymnal Hinos de Louvor e Súplicas a Deus
A Calvinist-leaning stress on God's election, from Francescon's Presbyterian past

profile.authority: The Bible, with the brief 'twelve articles of faith' and guidance believed to come from the Holy Spirit.
profile.salvation: Salvation by God's grace through faith in Christ, with a strong emphasis on God's election and calling.
profile.sacraments: Baptism of believers by immersion and the Santa Ceia (Holy Supper), celebrated once a year in each congregation.
profile.eschatology: Christ's return to gather the church, the resurrection and final judgement.
profile.governance: Elders and other ministers serve without pay; a council of elders in São Paulo (Brás) guides the church.
profile.worship: Hymns by number with orchestra, spontaneous prayer and preaching by those moved by the Spirit, without prepared sermons.

traditions.status: Active; the 2010 Brazilian census counted about 2.3 million members.

traditions.name: The Church of Pentecost (Ghana)
traditions.summary: Ghana's largest Protestant church, founded by the Irish missionary James McKeown, who arrived in the Gold Coast in 1937 for the Apostolic Church of Bradford. After disputes with the parent church in 1953 he and most Ghanaian members formed the Gold Coast Apostolic Church, renamed the Church of Pentecost in 1962. Under Ghanaian leaders since McKeown's retirement in 1982 it has spread through West Africa and the African diaspora.
distinctives: Leadership by apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, elders and deacons
Strong unpaid lay leadership by elders and deacons
Self-supporting from the start, with little foreign funding
Pentecost International Worship Centres (PIWC) for English-speaking and international congregations
Missions in more than a hundred countries
Pentecost University in Accra

profile.authority: The Bible as the inspired Word of God, with the Apostolic Church's Tenets of faith.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through faith in Christ, with emphasis on holy living.
profile.sacraments: Believer's baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper as a memorial.
profile.eschatology: Premillennial; the Rapture of the church and Christ's return.
profile.governance: A centralised church led by a Chairman, General Secretary and Executive Council, with apostles over regions and pastors posted by the church.
profile.worship: Lively Pentecostal worship in Twi and other languages, with prayer for healing and deliverance.

traditions.status: Active and growing in Ghana and worldwide.

traditions.name: Deeper Christian Life Ministry
traditions.summary: A Nigerian holiness-Pentecostal church that began in August 1973 as a Bible study held by William F. Kumuyi, a mathematics lecturer at the University of Lagos, in his flat in Yaba. Kumuyi, who came from Anglican and Methodist backgrounds and was influenced by the Apostolic Faith church, stressed strict holiness, restitution and Bible teaching. The Deeper Life Bible Church was formally set up in 1982 and grew into one of Nigeria's largest churches.
distinctives: Teaching on entire sanctification as a distinct work of grace
Strict standards of dress and conduct, relaxed somewhat since the 2010s
Weekly Monday Bible study and Thursday miracle services
House fellowships for pastoral care
Restitution for past wrongs as part of repentance
Global crusades led by Kumuyi

profile.authority: The Bible as the inerrant Word of God, taught systematically.
profile.salvation: Repentance and faith in Christ for salvation, followed by sanctification and the baptism in the Holy Spirit.
profile.sacraments: Baptism of believers by immersion and the Lord's Supper as a memorial.
profile.eschatology: Premillennial, with the Rapture before the Great Tribulation; strong expectation of Christ's return.
profile.governance: Led by a General Superintendent, with regional overseers and pastors.
profile.worship: Simple, Bible-centred services with hymns, prayer and long teaching sessions.

traditions.status: Active in Nigeria and in many countries in Africa and the diaspora.

traditions.name: Apostolic Faith Mission of South Africa
traditions.summary: South Africa's oldest and largest classical Pentecostal church, begun in Johannesburg in 1908 by the American missionaries John G. Lake and Thomas Hezmalhalch, who had links with Azusa Street and with John Alexander Dowie's Zion movement. Registered in 1913, it was organised for decades in separate racial sections under apartheid, which were united into one church in 1996.
distinctives: Roots in both Azusa Street and Dowie's Zion healing movement
Strong emphasis on divine healing
Racial divisions under apartheid, ended by union in 1996
Produced David du Plessis, 'Mr Pentecost' of the ecumenical charismatic movement
Influence on the Zionist African Initiated Churches

profile.authority: The Bible as the Word of God, with the church's confession of faith.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through faith in Christ, followed by baptism in the Holy Spirit.
profile.sacraments: Believer's baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper as a memorial.
profile.governance: National office-bearers and regions, with local assemblies led by pastors and elders.
profile.worship: Pentecostal worship with prayer for healing, in English, Afrikaans and African languages.

traditions.status: Active; a major church in South Africa with work in neighbouring countries.

traditions.name: Evangelical Lutheran Church in Tanzania (ELCT)
traditions.summary: One of the largest Lutheran churches in the world, formed in 1963 by the union of seven regional Lutheran churches that had grown from German missions (Berlin, Leipzig and Bethel) from the late nineteenth century, and from Scandinavian and American work after the First World War. It is organised in dioceses under bishops and a presiding bishop, and runs major hospitals, schools and universities.
distinctives: Dioceses led by bishops, with a presiding bishop
Large network of hospitals, including Kilimanjaro Christian Medical Centre
Tumaini University and Makumira University
Strong influence of the East African Revival in some dioceses
Bishop Josiah Kibira became the first African President of the Lutheran World Federation (1977)
Women ordained in some dioceses but not others

profile.authority: Scripture as the Word of God, with the ecumenical creeds, the Augsburg Confession and Luther's Small Catechism.
profile.salvation: Justification by grace through faith in Christ, preached as Law and Gospel.
profile.sacraments: Baptism, including infants, and the Lord's Supper with the real presence of Christ.
profile.governance: Episcopal: dioceses with bishops, a presiding bishop and a general assembly.
profile.worship: Lutheran liturgy in Swahili and local languages, with choirs and lively singing.

traditions.status: Active and growing; a leading member of the Lutheran World Federation.

traditions.name: Ethiopian Kale Heywet Church
traditions.summary: A large Ethiopian evangelical church that grew from the work of the Sudan Interior Mission (SIM), whose missionaries, including Thomas Lambie and Walter Ohman, began work in southern Ethiopia in 1927. When the Italian occupation expelled the missionaries in 1937, a handful of believers in Wolaitta grew into thousands of believers under local leadership, a story told in Raymond Davis's Fire on the Mountains. The name 'Kale Heywet' means 'Word of Life'.
distinctives: Rapid indigenous growth during the Italian occupation (1936–1941)
Strong in the south among Wolaitta, Kambatta, Hadiya, Sidama and Gedeo peoples
Endured persecution under the Derg (1974–1991)
Evangelical theology with growing charismatic renewal
Extensive Bible schools and development work

profile.authority: Scripture as the inspired and authoritative Word of God.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through faith in Christ, with emphasis on conversion and holy living.
profile.sacraments: Ordinances of believer's baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper as a memorial.
profile.governance: Local congregations grouped in district and regional associations under a national general assembly.
profile.worship: Lively evangelical worship in local languages, with choirs and prayer.

traditions.status: Active; one of Ethiopia's largest Protestant churches, alongside Mekane Yesus.

traditions.name: Evangelical Presbyterian Church of Egypt (Coptic Evangelical Church)
traditions.summary: Egypt's largest Protestant church, also called the Synod of the Nile, which grew from the mission of the American United Presbyterian Church begun in 1854. Most of its members came from Coptic Orthodox families, which is why it is often called the Coptic Evangelical Church. It is known for schools, the Evangelical Theological Seminary in Cairo, and Kasr el Dobara Evangelical Church near Tahrir Square, the largest Protestant congregation in the Middle East.
distinctives: Arab Presbyterian church drawn mainly from Coptic families
Strong educational tradition, including the Evangelical Theological Seminary in Cairo
Social service through CEOSS (founded by Samuel Habib in 1950)
Kasr el Dobara Church, which served as a field clinic in the 2011 revolution
Leading member of the Protestant Churches of Egypt

profile.authority: Scripture as the Word of God, with the Westminster Confession as a subordinate standard.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through faith in Christ, in Reformed theology.
profile.sacraments: Baptism, including infants, and the Lord's Supper in which Christ is spiritually present.
profile.governance: Presbyterian: sessions, presbyteries and the Synod of the Nile.
profile.worship: Arabic Reformed worship with hymns, contemporary songs and preaching.

traditions.status: Active; the main Protestant church in Egypt.

traditions.name: Newfrontiers and British Apostolic Networks
traditions.summary: Networks of charismatic churches that grew from the British 'House Church' or Restoration movement of the 1970s, which sought to restore apostles and prophets to the church. The best known is Newfrontiers, led by Terry Virgo from Brighton, which joined Reformed theology with charismatic worship. Similar networks included Bryn Jones's Covenant Ministries, Gerald Coates's Pioneer and Barney Coombs's Salt and Light. Since 2011 Newfrontiers has worked as several apostolic 'spheres'.
distinctives: Recognition of present-day apostles who oversee networks of churches
Reformed theology with charismatic gifts ('charismatic Calvinism')
Male eldership in local churches
Strong emphasis on church planting
Large Bible weeks, such as Stoneleigh (1991–2001)

profile.authority: Scripture as the inspired Word of God; apostolic and prophetic ministry is under its authority.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through faith, often in a Reformed framework.
profile.sacraments: Believer's baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper as a memorial.
profile.eschatology: Hopeful about the growth of the church before Christ's return; amillennial and postmillennial views are common.
profile.governance: Elder-led local churches linked to apostolic teams.
profile.worship: Charismatic worship with bands, spiritual gifts and expository preaching.

traditions.status: Active; Newfrontiers 'spheres' and related networks lead churches in many countries.

traditions.name: GAFCON (Global Anglican Future Conference)
traditions.summary: A movement of conservative Anglicans begun at the Global Anglican Future Conference in Jerusalem in June 2008, after disputes over sexuality and authority that followed Lambeth Resolution I.10 (1998) and the consecration of Gene Robinson in 2003. Its Jerusalem Declaration states its doctrine. Supported by large provinces in Africa, especially Nigeria, Uganda, Kenya and Rwanda, it recognised the Anglican Church in North America and set up structures for conservatives in other provinces. In 2023 its Kigali Commitment rejected the leadership of the Archbishop of Canterbury, and in October 2025 its leaders said they would reorder as a 'Global Anglican Communion'.
distinctives: The Jerusalem Declaration (2008) as a confessional statement
The Thirty-Nine Articles and the 1662 Book of Common Prayer as standards
Traditional teaching on marriage and sexuality
Support for alternative provinces such as ACNA
Rejection of Canterbury's leadership of the Communion (Kigali, 2023)
Leadership chiefly from the Global South

profile.authority: Scripture as the final authority, read in its plain sense, with the creeds, the first four councils, the Thirty-Nine Articles and the 1662 Prayer Book.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through faith in Christ's atoning death, as in the Thirty-Nine Articles.
profile.sacraments: The two gospel sacraments of baptism, including infants, and the Lord's Supper.
profile.eschatology: Christ's return, resurrection and judgement, as in the creeds.
profile.governance: Episcopal: a council of primates and a general secretary oversees member provinces and branches.
profile.worship: Prayer Book worship, often combined with contemporary evangelical or charismatic styles.
profile.canon: The 66-book Protestant canon; the Apocrypha is read for example but not for doctrine.

traditions.status: Active; it claims to represent most of the world's Anglicans, and its relations with the Anglican Communion are changing.

denomProfiles.tagline: Independent, evangelical congregations without a denominational label, often large and contemporary.
coreDoctrines: Authority and inspiration of the Bible
Salvation by grace through personal faith in Christ
focuses: Evangelism and reaching people unused to church
practices: Baptism by immersion, sometimes in large public services

influencedBy.name: Evangelicalism
influencedBy.text: Shares the conversionist, Bible-centred faith of the wider evangelical movement.

influencedBy.name: Charismatic Renewal
influencedBy.text: Many congregations adopted charismatic worship and expect spiritual gifts.

influencedBy.name: Calvary Chapel
influencedBy.text: Its informal Jesus Movement style shaped later independent churches.

influencedBy.name: Church-growth movement
influencedBy.text: Donald McGavran and later 'seeker-sensitive' models shaped strategy and style.

influenced.name: Global independent churches
influenced.text: Megachurch models and resources have been widely copied in Africa, Asia and Latin America.

influenced.name: Contemporary worship music
influenced.text: Large independent churches have become major producers of worship songs.

keyFigures.name: Bill Hybels
keyFigures.role: Founded Willow Creek Community Church (1975), the model 'seeker' church; resigned in 2018 amid misconduct allegations.

keyFigures.name: Joel Osteen
keyFigures.role: Pastor of Lakewood Church, Houston, one of the largest US congregations.

keyFigures.name: Andy Stanley
keyFigures.role: Founded North Point Community Church, Atlanta (1995).

denomProfiles.inIndia: Independent and non-denominational congregations are very common in Indian cities, including Chennai and other towns in Tamil Nadu and Kerala; many are Pentecostal-charismatic in style, and no reliable national count exists.

denomProfiles.tagline: Calvinistic Baptists bound by the 1689 Second London Confession.
coreDoctrines: The Lord's Day as the Christian Sabbath
focuses: Recovery of Puritan and Particular Baptist writings
practices: Use of Keach's Catechism (1693) and the 1689 Confession
Psalms and hymns, often without performance-style music

influencedBy.name: Particular Baptists
influencedBy.text: The movement claims direct continuity with the seventeenth-century Calvinistic Baptists.

influencedBy.name: Puritanism
influencedBy.text: Puritan theology, especially John Owen's, is heavily read.

influencedBy.name: Banner of Truth Trust
influencedBy.text: Founded in 1957, its reprints of Reformed classics spread the movement.

influenced.name: Southern Baptist Convention
influenced.text: The 'Young, Restless, Reformed' Calvinist resurgence among Southern Baptists drew on Reformed Baptist writing.

influenced.name: Reformed Baptist churches in Africa and Asia
influenced.text: Churches in Kenya, Nigeria, the Philippines and elsewhere have adopted the 1689 Confession.

keyFigures.name: Benjamin Keach
keyFigures.role: Seventeenth-century Particular Baptist pastor whose catechism is still used.

keyFigures.name: Charles Haddon Spurgeon
keyFigures.role: Reissued the 1689 Confession for his congregation in 1855.

keyFigures.name: Erroll Hulse
keyFigures.role: English pastor and editor of Reformation Today (from 1970).

keyFigures.name: Walter Chantry
keyFigures.role: American Reformed Baptist pastor and author.

denomProfiles.tagline: Old School Baptists: predestinarian, anti-mission and a cappella.
coreDoctrines: Regeneration as God's direct work, not caused by human means
No human institutions beyond the local church
practices: Monthly or regular communion with foot washing

influencedBy.name: Particular Baptists
influencedBy.text: They inherited Calvinistic confessions from the earlier Particular Baptists.

influencedBy.name: John Gill
influencedBy.text: Gill's high Calvinism shaped their teaching.

influencedBy.name: Anti-mission movement
influencedBy.text: Leaders such as Joshua Lawrence opposed the new mission boards of the 1820s.

influenced.name: Sacred Harp singing
influenced.text: Some Primitive Baptist communities helped preserve shape-note singing.

influenced.name: Primitive Baptist Universalists
influenced.text: A small Appalachian group that grew out of the movement.

keyFigures.name: Joshua Lawrence
keyFigures.role: North Carolina elder who led the anti-mission protest in the Kehukee Association.

keyFigures.name: Gilbert Beebe
keyFigures.role: Editor of the Signs of the Times (from 1832), the main Old School Baptist paper.

denomProfiles.tagline: Plain-living, horse-and-buggy Mennonites keeping nineteenth-century church order.
coreDoctrines: Non-resistance (refusal of violence and military service)
Humility and submission to the community
practices: Foot washing and the holy kiss

influencedBy.name: Mennonite Churches
influencedBy.text: They are a conservative branch of the Swiss–South German Mennonites.

influencedBy.name: Dordrecht Confession
influencedBy.text: The 1632 Dutch Mennonite confession remains their standard.

influenced.name: Amish
influenced.text: Old Order Amish and Old Order Mennonites share a similar resistance to modernity.

influenced.name: Conservative Mennonite groups
influenced.text: Later conservative splits drew on the Old Order example.

keyFigures.name: Jacob Wisler
keyFigures.role: Indiana bishop whose 1872 separation began the Old Order movement.

keyFigures.name: Abraham Martin
keyFigures.role: Leader of the Ontario Old Order separation (1889).

keyFigures.name: Jonas Martin
keyFigures.role: Lancaster County bishop who led the 1893 separation.

denomProfiles.tagline: Evangelical Mennonites born of an 1860 revival in Russia.
coreDoctrines: The church as a community of believers
practices: Conference cooperation in missions and schools

influencedBy.name: Mennonite Churches
influencedBy.text: They arose as a renewal movement among Russian Mennonites.

influencedBy.name: German Pietism
influencedBy.text: Eduard Wüst's revival preaching shaped the founders.

influencedBy.name: Baptist Churches
influencedBy.text: German Baptists influenced their adoption of immersion.

influenced.name: Mennonite Brethren churches in India
influenced.text: The missions produced one of the largest MB conferences worldwide.

influenced.name: Congolese Mennonite Brethren
influenced.text: The church in the DR Congo grew to be among the largest in the family.

keyFigures.name: Eduard Wüst
keyFigures.role: Pietist preacher whose revival inspired the founders.

keyFigures.name: Johann Claassen
keyFigures.role: Early leader who secured the group's legal recognition.

keyFigures.name: Abraham and Maria Friesen
keyFigures.role: Pioneer missionaries among the Telugu in India from 1889.

denomProfiles.inIndia: Mennonite Brethren work among Telugu speakers began in 1889; the Mennonite Brethren churches of Telangana and Andhra Pradesh, centred on Shamshabad, Mahbubnagar and Jadcherla, are among the largest MB bodies worldwide.

denomProfiles.tagline: Strictly confessional American Lutherans with a firm doctrine of fellowship.
coreDoctrines: Inerrancy and verbal inspiration of Scripture
Real presence of Christ in the Lord's Supper
Unity in doctrine as the basis of fellowship

influencedBy.name: Lutheran Churches
influencedBy.text: WELS stands in the confessional Lutheran tradition.

influencedBy.name: Martin Luther
influencedBy.text: Luther's catechisms and theology are central to its teaching.

influencedBy.name: Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod
influencedBy.text: Fellowship within the Synodical Conference (1872–1961) shaped its theology.

influenced.name: Evangelical Lutheran Synod
influenced.text: A close partner in the Confessional Evangelical Lutheran Conference.

influenced.name: Confessional Evangelical Lutheran Conference
influenced.text: WELS helped found this international body in 1993.

keyFigures.name: John Muehlhaeuser
keyFigures.role: First president and founder (1850).

keyFigures.name: Adolf Hoenecke
keyFigures.role: Theologian who made the synod strictly confessional.

keyFigures.name: John Philipp Koehler
keyFigures.role: Leader of the exegetical 'Wauwatosa theology'.

denomProfiles.tagline: Machen's church: strict Westminster Presbyterianism born of the 1936 split.

influencedBy.name: Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.)
influencedBy.text: Its founders left the northern Presbyterian church, a predecessor of the PC(USA).

influencedBy.name: Old Princeton theology
influencedBy.text: Charles Hodge and B. B. Warfield shaped Machen's thought.

influencedBy.name: Christianity and Liberalism
influencedBy.text: Machen's 1923 book argued that liberalism was a different religion.

influenced.name: Presbyterian Church in America
influenced.text: OPC theology and ministers influenced the PCA, founded in 1973.

influenced.name: Bible Presbyterian Church
influenced.text: A 1937 split led by Carl McIntire.

influenced.name: Reformed apologetics
influenced.text: Van Til's presuppositionalism spread through evangelicalism.

keyFigures.name: J. Gresham Machen
keyFigures.role: Founder and leading critic of liberal theology.

keyFigures.name: Cornelius Van Til
keyFigures.role: Apologist at Westminster Seminary.

keyFigures.name: John Murray
keyFigures.role: Scottish-born systematic theologian.

denomProfiles.tagline: Scottish Presbyterians of the 1843 Disruption, defending the church's spiritual independence.
coreDoctrines: Christ alone as head of the church

influencedBy.name: Church of Scotland
influencedBy.text: The Free Church separated from it in 1843.

influencedBy.name: Covenanters
influencedBy.text: Covenanting ideals of the church's independence shaped the Disruption.

influencedBy.name: Evangelical party
influencedBy.text: The Evangelical party in the Kirk under Chalmers led the protest.

influenced.name: Church of South India
influenced.text: Free Church missions in Madras fed into the united church.

influenced.name: Church of North India
influenced.text: Its missions in Bombay, Nagpur and Calcutta fed into the united church.

influenced.name: Free Church of Scotland (Continuing)
influenced.text: A minority that separated in 2000.

keyFigures.name: Thomas Chalmers
keyFigures.role: Leader of the Disruption and first Moderator.

keyFigures.name: Robert Candlish
keyFigures.role: Leading Free Church minister after Chalmers.

keyFigures.name: Alexander Duff
keyFigures.role: Missionary educator in Calcutta who joined the Free Church in 1843.

keyFigures.name: Thomas Guthrie
keyFigures.role: Preacher and pioneer of 'ragged schools'.

denomProfiles.inIndia: At the Disruption nearly all the Church of Scotland's missionaries in India joined the Free Church, including Alexander Duff in Calcutta, John Anderson in Madras (whose school became Madras Christian College) and John Wilson in Bombay; these missions later joined the Church of South India and the Church of North India.

denomProfiles.tagline: Covenanter Presbyterians singing psalms only and proclaiming Christ's kingship over nations.
coreDoctrines: Christ's kingship over church and state
Covenanting as a duty of churches and nations
focuses: Witness to Christ's rule in public life
practices: Close communion with tokens or interviews

influencedBy.name: Church of Scotland
influencedBy.text: The Covenanters were part of the Scottish Kirk before 1690.

influencedBy.name: National Covenant
influencedBy.text: The 1638 National Covenant and 1643 Solemn League and Covenant are their founding documents.

influencedBy.name: Samuel Rutherford
influencedBy.text: His Lex, Rex (1644) argued for the limits of royal power.

influenced.name: Free Church of Scotland
influenced.text: Covenanting ideals of spiritual independence fed into the Disruption.

influenced.name: American abolitionism
influenced.text: RPCNA members were early opponents of slavery in the United States.

keyFigures.name: Richard Cameron
keyFigures.role: Field preacher killed at Airds Moss in 1680.

keyFigures.name: James Renwick
keyFigures.role: Last Covenanter executed (1688).

keyFigures.name: John McMillan
keyFigures.role: Founding minister of the Reformed Presbytery (1743).

denomProfiles.tagline: Restorationist churches stressing discipleship, immersion baptism and church planting in world cities.
coreDoctrines: Discipleship as the mark of a true Christian

influencedBy.name: Churches of Christ
influencedBy.text: The movement began within the a cappella Churches of Christ.

influencedBy.name: Crossroads Movement
influencedBy.text: Chuck Lucas's Gainesville campus ministry developed its discipling method.

influenced.name: International Christian Church
influenced.text: Founded by Kip McKean in 2006 as a separate group.

influenced.name: Debate on spiritual abuse
influenced.text: Its early history became a major case study of high-demand church practices.

keyFigures.name: Kip McKean
keyFigures.role: Founder and leader until 2001.

keyFigures.name: Chuck Lucas
keyFigures.role: Minister of the Crossroads Church of Christ.

keyFigures.name: Henry Kriete
keyFigures.role: Leader whose 2003 letter prompted reform.

denomProfiles.inIndia: ICOC congregations meet in several major Indian cities, including Mumbai, Delhi, Chennai and Bengaluru, mainly among students and young professionals.

denomProfiles.tagline: Brazil's oldest Pentecostal church: unpaid elders, orchestras and no publicity.
coreDoctrines: Baptism in the Holy Spirit with speaking in tongues
practices: Men and women sit apart; women wear veils
Holy kiss between members of the same sex

influencedBy.name: Pentecostalism
influencedBy.text: Born of the early Pentecostal revival in Chicago.

influencedBy.name: William Durham
influencedBy.text: Durham's 'finished work' teaching shaped Francescon.

influencedBy.name: Italian Presbyterianism
influencedBy.text: Francescon was formerly an Italian Presbyterian, which explains the stress on election.

influenced.name: Italian Pentecostal churches
influenced.text: Francescon's circle also began churches among Italians in the United States, Italy and Argentina.

influenced.name: Brazilian Pentecostalism
influenced.text: As the first Pentecostal church in Brazil (with the Assembleias de Deus from 1911) it opened the way for later growth.

keyFigures.name: Louis Francescon
keyFigures.role: Founder (1910).

keyFigures.name: Giacomo Lombardi
keyFigures.role: Co-worker who went with Francescon to Argentina and Brazil.

denomProfiles.tagline: Ghana's largest Pentecostal church, self-supporting and led by apostles and lay elders.
coreDoctrines: Baptism in the Holy Spirit with speaking in tongues
The five-fold ministry of apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers
focuses: Holiness and moral teaching in society
practices: Weekly prayer meetings and all-night prayer

influencedBy.name: The Apostolic Church
influencedBy.text: McKeown brought its theology and offices of apostle and prophet.

influencedBy.name: Faith Tabernacle and Peter Anim
influencedBy.text: Peter Anim's earlier Gold Coast movement prepared the way.

influenced.name: African diaspora churches
influenced.text: Its congregations serve Ghanaians in Europe and North America.

influenced.name: Ghanaian Pentecostalism
influenced.text: Its discipline and missionary zeal shaped other Ghanaian churches.

keyFigures.name: James McKeown
keyFigures.role: Founder and first Chairman (1937–1982).

keyFigures.name: Opoku Onyinah
keyFigures.role: Chairman 2008–2018 and scholar of Pentecostal exorcism.

keyFigures.name: Eric Nyamekye
keyFigures.role: Chairman from 2018.

denomProfiles.tagline: Nigerian holiness-Pentecostal church of Bible study and strict sanctification.

influencedBy.name: Holiness Movement
influencedBy.text: Its doctrine of sanctification comes from Wesleyan holiness teaching.

influencedBy.name: Apostolic Faith Church
influencedBy.text: The Portland-based holiness-Pentecostal church shaped Kumuyi's theology.

influencedBy.name: Pentecostalism
influencedBy.text: It teaches baptism in the Holy Spirit.

influenced.name: Nigerian campus ministries
influenced.text: Its Bible studies influenced student Christianity in the 1970s and 1980s.

influenced.name: Nigerian holiness churches
influenced.text: Its strict ethic shaped other holiness-minded congregations.

keyFigures.name: William F. Kumuyi
keyFigures.role: Founder and General Superintendent.

denomProfiles.tagline: South Africa's pioneer Pentecostal church, from Lake's 1908 mission to post-apartheid unity.

influencedBy.name: Pentecostalism
influencedBy.text: Lake and Hezmalhalch brought the Azusa Street revival message.

influencedBy.name: Zion movement
influencedBy.text: John Alexander Dowie's healing movement shaped its early leaders.

influenced.name: African Initiated Churches
influenced.text: Many Zionist churches came from early AFM work.

influenced.name: Charismatic Renewal

keyFigures.role: American missionary and co-founder (1908).

keyFigures.name: Pieter L. le Roux
keyFigures.role: First South African president (1913–1943).

keyFigures.name: David du Plessis
keyFigures.role: General secretary and later ecumenical Pentecostal spokesman.

keyFigures.name: Frank Chikane
keyFigures.role: AFM pastor and anti-apartheid church leader.

denomProfiles.tagline: A large East African Lutheran church known for its bishops, hospitals and choirs.
coreDoctrines: Real presence in the Lord's Supper

influencedBy.name: Lutheran Churches
influencedBy.text: It grew from German, Scandinavian and American Lutheran missions.

influencedBy.name: East African Revival
influencedBy.text: The revival brought personal confession and fellowship to many congregations.

influenced.name: Lutheran World Federation

influenced.name: African Lutheran churches
influenced.text: It supports Lutheran work in neighbouring countries.

keyFigures.name: Stefano Moshi
keyFigures.role: First presiding bishop of the united church.

keyFigures.name: Josiah Kibira
keyFigures.role: Bishop of Bukoba and LWF President (1977–1984).

practices: Local evangelists sent out by congregations

influencedBy.name: Evangelicalism
influencedBy.text: SIM missionaries brought interdenominational evangelical faith.

influencedBy.name: Sudan Interior Mission
influencedBy.text: The mission's 'faith mission' approach shaped its early life.

influenced.name: Ethiopian Protestantism

influenced.name: Mission from Ethiopia
influenced.text: It sends evangelists to other regions and countries.

keyFigures.name: Thomas Lambie
keyFigures.role: SIM missionary leader in Ethiopia.

keyFigures.name: Walter Ohman
keyFigures.role: SIM missionary in Wolaitta.

keyFigures.name: Raymond Davis
keyFigures.role: SIM leader and author of Fire on the Mountains.

denomProfiles.tagline: Egypt's Presbyterian church, rooted in American missions and Coptic families.
coreDoctrines: Christ's spiritual presence in the Lord's Supper

influencedBy.name: Presbyterian Churches
influencedBy.text: It began through the American United Presbyterian mission.

influencedBy.name: Coptic Orthodox Church
influencedBy.text: Most early members came from Coptic families.

influenced.name: Coptic Orthodox Sunday School Movement

influenced.name: Arab Protestantism
influenced.text: Its seminary trains pastors for other Arab churches.

keyFigures.name: Samuel Habib
keyFigures.role: Founder of CEOSS and later head of the Protestant Churches of Egypt.

keyFigures.name: Andrea Zaki
keyFigures.role: President of the Protestant Churches of Egypt.

denomProfiles.tagline: British charismatic church networks led by apostles, joining Reformed teaching with spiritual gifts.
coreDoctrines: Baptism in the Holy Spirit and spiritual gifts
The church as God's central plan

influencedBy.name: Charismatic Renewal
influencedBy.text: The networks grew from the renewal of the 1960s and 1970s.

influencedBy.name: Reformed theology

influenced.name: Evangelical church planting

influenced.name: Charismatic Reformed churches

keyFigures.role: Founder of Newfrontiers.

keyFigures.name: Arthur Wallis

keyFigures.name: Bryn Jones
keyFigures.role: Leader of Covenant Ministries.

keyFigures.name: Gerald Coates
keyFigures.role: Founder of Pioneer.

denomProfiles.tagline: Global conservative Anglican movement founded in Jerusalem in 2008.
focuses: Support for conservative Anglicans in liberal provinces
practices: Consecration of bishops for conservative networks

influencedBy.name: Church of Nigeria

influencedBy.name: Church of Uganda
influencedBy.text: A strong supporter of GAFCON.

influencedBy.name: Anglican Church of Kenya
influencedBy.text: Hosted GAFCON 2013 in Nairobi.

influencedBy.name: Evangelicalism
influencedBy.text: Most of its leaders are evangelical.

influenced.text: Recognised by GAFCON as a province in 2009.

influenced.name: Anglican Network in Europe
influenced.text: Set up for conservatives in Britain and Europe.
